title: Shadow control-plane phased merge playbook
content:
Summary:
This is a working playbook for performing zero-to-low-downtime merges of a new control plane runtime into existing VPC / on-prem private deployments using a shadow-and-merge approach. The goal is to safely introduce a newer control-plane version and runtime components while preserving API compatibility and providing deterministic rollback paths. This document mixes operational steps, Terraform module notes, preflight checks, and explicit rollback recipes.

Scope and objectives:
- Scope: private-deployments (VPC and on-prem appliance customers) where a control-plane and serving runtime upgrade requires state reconciliation and API stability guarantees.
- Success criteria: 99.95% request success rate during transition window; no irreversible data migrations without an automated undo; all customer endpoints remain available or automatically routed to a safe fallback.
- Constraints: heterogeneous hardware, some air-gapped sites, limited maintenance windows for enterprise customers.

Assumptions:
- Remote state backend exists (S3/GCS with locking or equivalent).
- CI/CD can run terraform plan/app and has a pre-production environment that mirrors production networking topology.
- We have recent application-level snapshots and DB backups retained per the retention policy.

Stakeholders & Roles:
- Migration lead: Aisha Patel (author) — responsible for orchestration and go/no-go.
- Infra ops on-call: Ethan Clarke — rollback executor.
- Release engineer: Maya Li — terraform plan/reconcile and artifact promotion.
- Customer liaison: Tomás Rivera — customer communications and maintenance windows.

High-level approach (phased merge):
1) Shadow control plane deployment: deploy new control-plane components into the cluster/host but keep them isolated (no traffic). Synchronize read-only state (cache of CRs, model catalog, and feature flags) from the live control plane using the state-mirroring bridge.
2) Validation plateau: run a battery of integration tests and state-drift checks against the shadow instance. Run compatibility smoke tests (API surface, auth, RBAC).
3) Progressive traffic split: inject small percentages of non-customer traffic (synthetic/QA) and then low-volume customer traffic using edge routing weights.
4) Controlled promotion: incrementally promote traffic while verifying metrics and invariants.
5) Merge finalization: switch control-plane leader election (if applicable) and promote the shadow instance to primary.
6) Observability & cleanup: keep both control planes until a defined stabilization period, then decommission the old control plane.

Preflight checklist (must pass before traffic split):
- Terraform plan shows only intended resource changes and no provider version surprises.
- Remote state lock test passed in CI and manual lock/unlock exercises documented.
- DB schema migration drifts evaluated; reversible migration path exists or snapshot available.
- Backups: object-store and database snapshots from within last 24 hours.
- Health endpoints (liveness, readiness) implemented and passing on shadow components.
- API contract regression tests: all legacy endpoints return expected responses to canonical prompts.
- KV/cache format compatibility tests run between old runtime and new runtime.

Terraform & infra notes (practical tips and snippets):
- Module versioning: pin modules with an explicit module_version variable and use a promotion process (e.g., bump module_version in a release branch, run plan in preprod, then merge).
- Provider pinning: set required_providers and provider "lock" file to avoid unplanned provider upgrades.
- State migration pattern (safe path):
  1) terraform state pull > state.json (backup)
  2) terraform plan -var-file=site-vars.tfvars -target=module.control_plane
  3) If resource renames are needed: terraform state mv old_resource new_resource (document mapping in migration doc)
- Remote state and locking: ensure S3/GCS backend has versioning enabled and DynamoDB lease table (or GCS equivalent) for locks.
- Workspaces: use separate workspaces for "shadow" and "primary" to avoid accidental apply to the live control plane.
- CI gating: require terraform plan approval from at least two reviewers and a green infra-integration test run before apply.

Example terraform snippet to pin a module and create shadow stack:
module "control_plane_shadow" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//control-plane?ref=v2.8.0"
  module_version = "v2.8.0-shadow-2026-02"
  cluster_name = var.cluster_name
  namespace = "redwood-shadow"
}

Testing & validation suite (what to run against shadow):
- Contract tests: exercise every public endpoint (create, read, update, delete flows where applicable). Verify semantic behavior for the most-used endpoints.
- Serving behavior: run sample LLM requests at realistic sequence lengths, check latency tails and token correctness numbers against baseline.
- KV and cache verification: write-read cycles that stress cache eviction policies and persistence across restarts.
- Authorization & IAM: token exchange flows and role-based access tests.
- Chaos checks: simulate process restart, network partition, and disk pressure on the shadow to ensure graceful degradation.

Compatibility matrix (developer-facing):
- API endpoint changes: annotate each endpoint with status: compatible | extended | deprecated | removed. For any extended/removed endpoints, provide compatibility shim options inside the proxy layer.
- Runtime persistence format: indicate whether on-disk or KV layout is forward/backward compatible. If not compatible, include an automated migration tool and a pre-migration dry-run mode.

Traffic promotion strategy (safety-first):
- Step 0: 0% customer traffic (shadow only).
- Step 1: 1-5% synthetic traffic for 30m while monitoring error rate, p95 latency, and token cost.
- Step 2: 5-10% low-risk tenant traffic (customers who agreed to early exposure) for 1h.
- Step 3: 25% for 2h if metrics stable.
- Step 4: 50% for 4h.
- Step 5: 100% and deprecate old control-plane after stabilization window (24–72h depending on customer risk profile).

Monitoring & rollback triggers (objective thresholds):
- Immediate rollback if: error rate increases >0.5% absolute and sustained for 5 minutes, or p99 latency increases by >50% compared to baseline for 10 minutes.
- Soft rollback (slow down promotion) if: p95 increases >25% or Token-per-request cost increases >20% without quality improvement.
- Any out-of-memory or data corruption surfaced in logs triggers an immediate plan to switch all traffic to old control-plane.

Rollback playbooks (fast and slow):
- Fast rollback (stateless path):
  1) Flip edge weight to route 100% to old control-plane via traffic manager.
  2) Scale down shadow components to zero-or-idle using terraform apply -auto-approve on shadow workspace.
  3) Re-run smoke tests on old control-plane to ensure resumed stability.
- Slow rollback (stateful or DB migration reversible):
  1) Pause promotion, disable leader election on shadow, and re-enable read replicas.
  2) Run the automated data reconcile script to roll back any shadow-side writes to the old schema (if a reversible migration was used).
  3) Run a partial restore from snapshot for the small set of affected tenants if necessary.

Emergency checklist for irreversible failures:
- If the new control-plane performed an irreversible DB schema change without a reversible migration:
  - Immediately notify legal & customer success for potential incident impact.
  - Enable read-only mode at edge to preserve data while teams triage.
  - Restore last known-good snapshot into an isolated cluster and redirect affected tenants there.

Post-migration housekeeping:
- Retain shadow workspace and logs for at least 30 days for forensics.
- Deprecation communication: send API deprecation notes to customers on schedule.
- Run a migration retrospective with infra, release, and SRE teams; capture lessons and update module docs.

Notes on long-living compatibility shims and API proxies:
- Rather than removing endpoints, prefer implementing adapter logic in the ingress/proxy where feasible. This buys time for clients with slow upgrade cycles.
- Track shim code in a module with a clear TTL and automated feature-flag gating so we can retire shims once client adoption reaches a threshold.

Appendix A: sample commands and quick references
- Backup remote state:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-terraform-state/prod.tfstate ./prod.tfstate.backup-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%MZ)
- Lock test (S3 + Dynamo):
  # run in CI job that simulates lock acquisition and release
  terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform plan -out=plan.tfout && terraform show -json plan.tfout > plan.json
- Snapshot DB (Postgres example):
  pg_dump -Fc -h db.internal -U redwood redwood_prod > redwood_prod_snapshot_$(date +%F).dump

Appendix B: Terraform module migration notes (do's and don'ts)
- DO: keep module interfaces stable; add optional arguments rather than changing required ones.
- DO: provide a migration wrapper module that maps old inputs to new inputs when renaming occurs.
- DON'T: rely on terraform provider implicit behavior for resource renames. Explicit state mv mapping reduces errors.
- DO: include a "dry-run" mode in migration scripts that simulates state changes and shows an export of the planned renames.

Open questions and follow-ups (tracked actions):
- Confirm whether on-prem appliance images require a drifted kernel-level tweak for the new runtime; schedule lab validation.
- Add a preflight "traffic shadow" stage to the console so customers can opt-in to low-volume early testing.
- Decide retention window for shadow logs (30 vs 90 days) based on incident triage policy.

This doc is intentionally prescriptive but still a draft. Use comments and inline suggestions in the PR linked above. If we decide to finalize, we will convert to a runbook with executable checkboxes and integrate into the RedOps playbook library.
